item.title: Africa's Lithium Moment: How Battery Demand Is Redrawing Investment and Influence
item.body:
A decade ago, the map of the global battery supply chain barely included Africa. Today it does — and the change happened faster than most forecasts allowed for.

Zimbabwe, which produced almost no lithium in 2020, is now the continent's largest producer and ranks among the world's more significant sources of hard-rock lithium. Mali began shipping concentrate from a major new mine after production started in late 2024. Ghana has permitted its first lithium project. Namibia, Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo all have deposits at various stages of study, dispute or early development.

The interesting question is no longer whether Africa matters to the energy transition. It is how much of the value the continent captures — and what that leverage is actually worth in a market that has proven far more volatile than the "critical minerals supercycle" narrative suggested.

## From rounding error to real supply

Africa's lithium output has gone from statistically negligible at the start of the decade to a meaningful single-digit share of global mine supply, most of it concentrated in a handful of operations.

**Zimbabwe** anchors the story. Chinese groups acquired or developed the country's main hard-rock assets — including projects at Bikita, Arcadia and Sabi Star — largely between 2021 and 2023, then built and commissioned them quickly. That speed is the point: the acquisitions were made near the top of the price cycle, and construction continued through the crash that followed.

**Mali** is the newest entrant of scale, with a large spodumene operation ramping up under Chinese ownership and a second, smaller project alongside it. **Ghana** approved a mining lease for its first lithium project on notably tougher fiscal terms than its historical gold agreements — higher royalties and a larger state equity position — a signal other governments in the region read closely.

The **DRC** holds what is generally described as one of the largest undeveloped hard-rock lithium deposits in the world, at Manono. It has also been held up for years by contested ownership claims and international arbitration, a reminder that a world-class geological asset and a bankable project are not the same thing. Partial commercial settlements and new investor interest, including from US-linked funds, moved the file forward in 2025, but production remains a future event.

## The bottleneck is not rocks — it is refining

Here is the structural fact that shapes everything else: mining is the least concentrated link in the battery chain.

Roughly 60% or more of the world's lithium chemical refining capacity sits in China, along with the great majority of cathode and anode production. For rare earths, Chinese concentration in separation and permanent-magnet manufacturing is higher still — commonly estimated at around 90% for finished magnets.

That asymmetry has two consequences. For African governments, it means exporting concentrate captures only a slice of the eventual value of a battery. For Western and Asian buyers, it means acquiring an equity stake in an African mine does not, by itself, deliver supply-chain security — the material may still transit a processing system they do not control.

It also explains why Chinese firms moved earliest and most aggressively. Vertically integrated buyers with existing refineries could underwrite mine development through a price collapse that made the same projects uninvestable for standalone miners dependent on spot markets.

## Rare earths run on a different clock

The two mineral stories are often bundled together, but they are not on the same timeline.

Africa's rare earth position is still mostly prospective. Advanced projects in Malawi, Tanzania, Angola and South Africa could become significant, and several have attracted offtake interest and government-backed financing. Very little is producing at scale today.

What accelerated that interest was policy, not geology. China introduced export controls covering rare earth extraction and separation technology, then expanded restrictions on certain heavy rare earths and magnet products in 2025 before a partial trade truce with Washington later that year suspended some measures temporarily. The episode made a point that industrial planners had underweighted: for rare earths, the scarce asset is separation and magnet-making capability, not ore in the ground. New African mines help only if non-Chinese midstream capacity is built to receive their output.

## Where the money is coming from — and in what form

Capital is arriving through visibly different instruments.

Chinese companies have generally deployed **direct equity and construction capital**, buying assets and building plants on commercial timelines.

The United States, European Union, Japan, South Korea and Gulf states have leaned more on **policy architecture and infrastructure**: the Lobito Corridor rail initiative linking Angola with the DRC and Zambia's copper belt; EU critical raw materials partnerships and Global Gateway financing; development-finance guarantees; sovereign-fund investments in mining assets; and long-term offtake agreements. This approach is slower to show up as tonnes but potentially more durable, because logistics and power are the real constraints on most African projects.

**Morocco** is the outlier worth studying. Rather than competing on lithium reserves, it has attracted battery-precursor, cathode and gigafactory investment by selling location and trade access — proximity to European carmakers plus preferential trade arrangements. It is currently the clearest example on the continent of moving up the value chain rather than simply out of the ground.

## Governments raising the price of entry

Resource nationalism, in its policy rather than rhetorical form, is now standard.

Zimbabwe banned exports of raw lithium ore in 2022 and has signalled it will eventually require concentrates to be processed domestically. Namibia restricted exports of several unprocessed critical minerals in 2023. Mali revised its mining code to increase state participation. The African Union adopted a continental green minerals strategy in 2025, and the DRC and Zambia have discussed joint battery-precursor manufacturing.

The DRC also demonstrated something sharper. As the source of roughly three-quarters of the world's mined cobalt, it suspended and then rationed exports through a quota system in 2025 — and prices moved substantially. That is genuine market power, exercised deliberately, in the one commodity where the continent's share is dominant rather than marginal.

Announcing downstream processing is easier than building it, though. Refineries need firm, cheap electricity, reliable water, skilled operators and enough throughput to compete with incumbent Chinese plants running at scale. Several announced lithium chemical facilities remain unbuilt or partially completed.

## The cycle cuts both ways

None of this happened against a stable price backdrop. Lithium chemical prices fell roughly 80% to 90% from their late-2022 peak, one of the sharper commodity reversals of the decade, before recovering part of the ground in 2025 as supply discipline tightened and demand kept growing.

The consequences were immediate: delayed final investment decisions, deferred expansions, mothballed capacity, and renegotiated timelines — including at some African projects that had been presented as near-term. Governments negotiating twenty-year fiscal terms and thirty-year rail concessions are doing so against a price signal that can halve in a year.

Anyone reading this space should treat both boom and bust framings with caution. Demand growth for storage and electric vehicles has been real and persistent; so has the industry's capacity to oversupply itself.

## What to watch next

- **Commissioning, not announcements.** Whether announced lithium sulphate and chemical plants in Zimbabwe and processing facilities in Nigeria actually reach production.
- **Manono.** Whether the DRC's flagship lithium deposit clears its legal overhang and begins construction.
- **Corridors and power.** Progress on the Lobito rail project and on grid reliability, which quietly determines whether refining onshore is viable.
- **Midstream outside China.** Whether separation and magnet capacity gets built in Europe, the US, Japan or Africa itself — the precondition for African rare earths to change anything strategically.
- **Chemistry drift.** Wider adoption of LFP, sodium-ion and improved recycling could soften lithium demand per kilowatt-hour, even as total demand rises.
- **Trade terms.** The lapse of long-standing US preferential trade access for African exports in late 2025, and how renewal discussions land, affects the calculus for manufacturing on the continent.
- **Transparency.** Contract disclosure and revenue reporting through mechanisms such as the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative remain the practical test of whether higher state takes translate into public benefit.

## Risks worth stating plainly

Rapid extraction growth brings familiar problems: water use and tailings management in already stressed catchments, community displacement and compensation disputes, safety in informal and artisanal mining, corruption exposure in licensing, and the enclave problem — mines that generate export revenue without generating local employment or industry.

Revenue volatility is its own governance risk. Budgets built on peak-cycle mineral receipts have historically been difficult to unwind.

## The bottom line

Africa's role in the battery economy is expanding genuinely, but unevenly. In cobalt, the continent already sets terms. In lithium, it has become a real supplier in five years — while remaining a price-taker in a market whose profits sit downstream. In rare earths, it holds promising deposits and very little of the processing capability that gives them strategic weight.

The comparison to earlier commodity scrambles is imperfect in one important way. African governments today face more competing buyers, hold more legal and fiscal instruments, and negotiate with better information than in previous booms. Whether that translates into industrial development rather than a faster extraction cycle is not a geological question. It depends on power stations, railways, contract terms and institutions — the unglamorous inputs that decide who captures value.
